query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide surface coating to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without degrading its inherent room‐ and elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that shows acceptable ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from pesting/oxidation in air at high temperature.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, uniform aluminide coating (for example, via pack cementation or a related vapor deposition method) on the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures around 800 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours (mimicking prior oxidation tests) while maintaining strain rates consistent with the baseline mechanical tests (10^–4–10^–2 s^–1) during any subsequent mechanical evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) scale on the surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the aluminide coating oxidizes preferentially to form a stable and slow-growing alumina layer. This protective Al₂O₃ scale serves as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress, thereby reducing the overall oxidation (pesting) of the underlying alloy while leaving its bulk mechanical properties largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminide-coated alloy will exhibit a markedly lower oxidation rate (e.g., reduced mass gain and surface degradation) during high-temperature air exposure compared to the uncoated alloy, and its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength will remain comparable to the baseline performance.
generation.baseline: Uncoated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which, despite its good mechanical performance, undergoes significant oxidation (pesting) under prolonged high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The intervention should be effective for temperatures up to about 800–1000 °C and for exposure durations of at least 5 hours in air; the coating must be thin enough not to alter the bulk properties and must remain stable during both thermal exposure and mechanical loading within the tested strain rate range.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, the long-term adhesion behavior at the alloy/coating interface, and any possible subtle diffusion interactions during prolonged thermal cycling remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the applied aluminide coating and one set left uncoated. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours in a controlled furnace. After exposure, perform comprehensive analyses including surface oxidation characterization (using SEM/EDS and XRD) and measure mass gain. Subsequently, conduct room- and high-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature and at 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated samples do not exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate (comparable or higher mass gain and oxide scale disruption) relative to the uncoated samples, or if the coating demonstrably degrades the alloy’s mechanical performance (significant loss in ductility or yield strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
